question: What is the main goal of a Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in a hospital?

options.A: To provide free medications to all visiting patients
options.B: To maintain a continuous supply of essential drugs through sales revenue
options.C: To fund the construction of new hospital wards and laboratories
options.D: To generate profit for the hospital management board

explanation: Think of the DRF like a self-sustaining cycle! Money from drug sales is used right back to buy fresh stock, so the pharmacy never runs dry. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h1)

question: What happens if money meant for the DRF is used to pay for unrelated hospital bills?

options.A: The prices of medicines in the hospital automatically decrease for all patients
options.B: The pharmacy runs out of stock because money is missing to buy new drugs
options.C: The pharmacy staff must pay for the missing inventory out of their own salaries
options.D: The government automatically replaces the missing funds within twenty-four hours

explanation: Because the DRF relies completely on its own cash flow, taking cash out for other projects breaks the cycle and leaves the shelves empty. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h1)

question: What does 'full cost recovery' mean when pricing drugs in a DRF?

options.A: Recovering the purchase price plus all operational expenses needed to supply the drug
options.B: Selling the drugs at the exact same price the manufacturer printed on the box
options.C: Charging double the market price to make a large profit for the clinic
options.D: Waiting for the government to refund the pharmacy after all drugs are sold out

explanation: It simply means the price covers not just what the supplier charged, but also the extra costs of bringing the medicine safely to the pharmacy. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h2)

question: Why must a pharmacy balance full cost recovery with making drugs affordable?

options.A: To prevent private pharmacies from suing the hospital for unfair competition
options.B: To ensure the doctors receive a bonus for prescribing cheaper medications
options.C: To comply with international laws governing pharmaceutical manufacturing
options.D: To make sure vulnerable patients can still afford their essential treatments

explanation: If drug prices climb too high, everyday patients won't be able to buy them, which defeats the whole public health mission of our hospitals. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which of these is a direct cost when buying medicines?

options.A: Monthly electricity bills for the pharmacy store
options.B: The invoice price paid to the drug manufacturer
options.C: Printing costs for general hospital stationery
options.D: Salaries paid to the hospital security guards

explanation: Direct costs are expenses tied directly to purchasing the actual pharmaceutical items—like the supplier's bill. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h3)

question: A hospital pharmacy prices an antibiotic by adding up the supplier price, shipping fees, storage power, and dispensing salaries. What costing approach is this?
explanation: Spot on! Including both the price of the drug and all overhead expenses ensures the fund gets back every kobo spent to deliver care. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h3)

question: What do logistics expenses cover in a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: The expenses involved in transporting, storing, and handling drugs safely
options.B: The cost of manufacturing raw chemical ingredients in a laboratory
options.C: The taxes paid by pharmaceutical companies on their annual profits
options.D: The clinical fees charged by nurses for administering injections

explanation: Logistics covers all the physical moving, warehousing, and care of medicines before they finally reach the clinic shelf. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h4)

question: Why must cold chain costs be included when calculating logistics for vaccines?

options.A: Refrigeration equipment requires ongoing power and servicing to keep products potent
options.B: Keeping vaccines cold increases their weight and doubles the shipping fees
options.C: Cold storage fees are paid directly to the patients who receive the vaccines
options.D: Government regulations prohibit charging patients for unrefrigerated medicines

explanation: Vaccines need steady refrigeration to stay active. Maintaining fuel and power adds real financial costs to the supply chain! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of adding a small 'sustainability mark-up' to DRF drugs?

options.A: To pay the personal salaries of the hospital medical director
options.B: To protect the fund against inflation, wastage, and future stock depletion
options.C: To generate heavy profits for private investors
options.D: To punish patients who do not pay their hospital bills on time

explanation: The sustainability margin acts as a safety cushion against rising market prices and expired items so the fund doesn't shrink. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is likely to happen if a hospital sets its DRF mark-up to zero percent?

options.A: The pharmacy will gradually lose purchasing power due to inflation and waste, leading to stock-outs
options.B: Patients will buy more drugs because they are cheaper, making the fund richer
options.C: The hospital will save money on administrative costs and paperwork
options.D: The government will send extra money every month to maintain the exact same inventory level

explanation: Without a small mark-up to cover waste and inflation, your capital gradually shrinks until you can no longer afford to restock. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h5)

question: What does 'replacement cost pricing' mean in a changing economy?

options.A: Waiting for the government to fix market prices before selling any drugs
options.B: Selling all medicines at half price when they are close to their expiration date
options.C: Pricing drugs based on how much it will cost to buy new stock tomorrow
options.D: Charging patients the exact same price the manufacturer set ten years ago

explanation: Replacement pricing ensures that the money you collect today is enough to buy brand-new stock at current market prices. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h6)

question: If the local currency drops in value, making imported drugs much more expensive, what should the DRF committee do?

options.A: Keep selling remaining stock at old prices until everything is completely gone
options.B: Borrow money from patients to pay for the next batch of imported drugs
options.C: Adjust selling prices based on current replacement costs to protect the fund
options.D: Stop selling medications entirely and wait for inflation to reverse itself naturally

explanation: If you don't adjust prices during currency drops, your sales revenue won't be enough to buy the next batch of drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h6)

question: What is the main reason for doing regular physical stock counts in a pharmacy?

options.A: To compare actual pills on the shelf with recorded ledger numbers
options.B: To calculate the annual bonus for the hospital accountant
options.C: To make the pharmacy staff work longer hours on the weekend
options.D: To dispose of all medications that have been on the shelf for one week

explanation: Counting actual stock helps catch issues like missing items, breakage, or recording mistakes early. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h7)

question: Why is tracking near-expiry drugs important for protecting a DRF?

options.A: It allows the pharmacy to redistribute or discount slow-moving stock before it spoils and wastes money
options.B: It ensures that expired medications can be repackaged with new expiration dates
options.C: It forces the manufacturer to refund the hospital for drugs that sell too quickly
options.D: It proves to the patients that the hospital only buys the freshest imported drugs

explanation: Catching drugs before they expire lets you transfer them or sell them off, saving the facility from losing hard-earned capital. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T4#GNS215_U3_T4_h7)
